question: What does a surety bond guarantee, and how is it different from insurance?
aliases: Is a surety bond the same thing as insurance?
What is the difference between being bonded and being insured?
If someone files a claim on my bond, do I have to pay the surety back?
Who does a surety bond actually protect, me or my customer?
shortAnswer: A surety bond guarantees that the bonded party will perform an obligation, and it is written for the party that required the bond rather than the party that pays for it. NASBP describes a surety bond as a promise to be liable for the debt, default, or failure of another, and as a three-party contract in which the surety guarantees the performance of the principal to the obligee, with the surety secondarily liable rather than assuming the primary obligation [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding]. When a surety pays, it expects the money back: California Civil Code section 2847 provides that if a surety satisfies the principal obligation, or any part of it, with or without legal proceedings, the principal is bound to reimburse what the surety has disbursed, including necessary costs and expenses, except as prescribed by the next section [S:ca-civ-code-2847-surety-reimbursement], and NASBP says the general agreement of indemnity is signed before the surety issues any bonds [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding]. Each bond is conditioned on a defined event written into that bond, so what a specific bond reaches is a question about that bond form and its penal sum [S:cfr-13-115-10-sba-definitions].
assumes: The subject is a commercial surety bond written by a surety company. Bail bonds are outside this article. California's Insurance Code also provides that no insurance may be written as surety insurance if it falls within the definition of financial guaranty insurance in section 12100 [S:ca-ins-code-105-surety-insurance].
The question is about general mechanics, not the reading of one specific bond form or the outcome of one specific claim. No bond form is quoted here, and no claim outcome is predicted.
Federal dollar figures are quoted as they appear in 40 U.S.C. 3131 and in FAR 28.102-1 as of 2026-08-31 [S:usc-40-3131-miller-act][S:far-28-102-1].

The California license bond discussion assumes a CSLB-licensed contractor. Section 7071.6(c) provides that a bond shall not be required of a holder of a license that has been inactivated on the official records of the board during the period the license is inactive [S:ca-bpc-7071-6-contractor-bond].
Nothing here is a coverage determination, an eligibility verdict, or legal advice about a particular bond, contract, or claim.
why:
Three parties, three roles. In the definitions SBA uses for its Surety Bond Guarantee Program, the principal is the person bidding for the award of a contract in the case of a bid bond, and the person primarily liable to complete the contract or to make contract-related payments in the case of a final or ancillary bond; the obligee for a final bond is the person who has contracted with the principal for completion of the contract and to whom the primary obligation of the surety runs in the event of a breach by the principal, and for a bid bond it is the person requesting bids; and the surety is a company that, under a bid bond, agrees to pay a sum of money to the obligee if the principal breaches the conditions of the bond, under a performance bond agrees to pay a sum of money or to incur the cost of fulfilling the terms of a contract, and under a payment or ancillary bond agrees to make payment to all who have a right of action against the bond [S:cfr-13-115-10-sba-definitions]. Those definitions are written for that program, but the structure is the same one NASBP describes for contract surety generally: a three-party contract in which the surety guarantees the performance of the principal to the obligee, with the bond given to the obligee, and roles that shift with position in the chain, so that if the owner is the obligee the prime contractor is the principal, and if the prime contractor is the obligee the subcontractor is the principal [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding].

A surety writes bonds expecting not to pay. NASBP states that a fundamental concept of suretyship is that the surety will not sustain a loss, that a surety does not expect to suffer losses because it expects the bonded principal to perform and because it holds a signed indemnity agreement, and that obtaining bonds is more like obtaining bank credit than purchasing insurance, with underwriting that weighs financial capacity, net worth, cash flow, assets, credit score, work in progress, work history, banking relationship, the nature of the project, and the character of the contractor [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding]. The general agreement of indemnity is the instrument that makes that expectation real. NASBP describes it as a contract obligating the contractor and other indemnitors to protect the surety from any loss or expense resulting from having issued bonds, needed before the surety issues any bonds and applying to all bonds it issues for that principal, and it says a surety almost always requires the principal, the individuals who own or control the company, their spouses, and often affiliated companies to sign it [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding].

In California the repayment duty is also statutory. Civil Code section 2847 provides that if a surety satisfies the principal obligation, or any part of it, whether with or without legal proceedings, the principal is bound to reimburse what the surety has disbursed, including necessary costs and expenses, and that the surety has no claim for reimbursement against other persons though they may have been benefited by its act, except as prescribed by the next section [S:ca-civ-code-2847-surety-reimbursement]. Two limits sit on the face of that text: the right depends on the surety having satisfied the principal obligation, and it is expressly subject to the following section. How section 2847 applies to a particular payment, and what a signed indemnity agreement adds on top of it, is a legal question for a lawyer.

Surety is a regulated class of insurance, which is not the same thing as being insurance for the bonded party. California's Insurance Code says surety insurance includes the guaranteeing of behavior of persons and the guaranteeing of performance of contracts, including executing or guaranteeing bonds and undertakings required or permitted in all actions or proceedings or by law allowed, other than insurance policies and other than payments secured by a mortgage, deed of trust, or other instrument constituting a lien or charge on real estate [S:ca-ins-code-105-surety-insurance]. Separately, a person shall not transact any class of insurance business in California without first being admitted for that class, and admission is secured by procuring a certificate of authority from the Insurance Commissioner [S:ca-ins-code-700-certificate-of-authority]. NASBP puts the practical contrast plainly: surety bonds are almost always written by insurance companies licensed by state insurance departments, but they are not like traditional insurance policies, because surety bonds are three-party agreements while traditional insurance policies such as life or property insurance are two-party agreements, and the surety does not assume the primary obligation but is secondarily liable if the principal defaults [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding].

So what does the bond do for the business that buys it. It answers to someone else. A payment on the bond runs to the obligee or to the persons who have a right of action against the bond [S:cfr-13-115-10-sba-definitions], and the principal and its indemnitors are legally bound to pay the surety back [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding][S:ca-civ-code-2847-surety-reimbursement]. What any particular bond reaches is set by the conditions written into that bond: in SBA's definitions, a performance bond is conditioned upon completion by the principal of a contract in accordance with its terms, a payment bond is conditioned upon payment by the principal of money to persons who have a right of action against the bond, and a bid bond is conditioned upon the bidder entering into the contract and furnishing the required payment and performance bonds [S:cfr-13-115-10-sba-definitions]. Amounts are bond-specific rather than general: NASBP says a surety's liability under a bid bond is generally limited to the face amount, or penal sum, of the bond, typically 5 to 20 percent of the contract bid price [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding], and SBA's rule for the bonds it guarantees is that a payment bond cannot require the surety to pay an amount exceeding the claimant's actual loss or damage [S:cfr-13-115-10-sba-definitions]. Whether a business also needs property, general liability, or workers compensation insurance is a separate question, answered by reading those policies and whatever contracts or statutes require them, not by reading the bond.

On federal construction work, bonds are statutory. 40 U.S.C. 3131(b) provides that before any contract of more than $100,000 is awarded for the construction, alteration, or repair of any public building or public work of the federal government, a person must furnish a performance bond with a surety satisfactory to the officer awarding the contract and in an amount the officer considers adequate for the protection of the government, and a payment bond with a surety satisfactory to the officer for the protection of all persons supplying labor and material in carrying out the work [S:usc-40-3131-miller-act]. The amount of the payment bond shall equal the total amount payable by the terms of the contract unless the awarding officer determines, in a writing supported by specific findings, that a payment bond in that amount is impractical, and it shall not be less than the amount of the performance bond [S:usc-40-3131-miller-act]. That requirement is not absolute in either direction. Subsection (d) lets a contracting officer waive the performance bond and payment bond requirement for work under a contract to be performed in a foreign country if the officer finds it is impracticable for the contractor to furnish the bonds, and subsection (e) provides that the section does not limit the contracting officer's authority to require a performance bond or other security in addition to those specified in subsection (b), or in cases other than the cases specified there [S:usc-40-3131-miller-act]. So the threshold is a floor for when bonds are required, not a ceiling on what an agency may ask for. The figure a contractor usually sees is the regulation's. FAR 28.102-1(a) states that 40 U.S.C. chapter 31, subchapter III requires performance and payment bonds for any construction contract exceeding $150,000, except that the requirement may be waived by the contracting officer for work performed in a foreign country upon a finding that it is impracticable for the contractor to furnish the bonds, or as otherwise authorized by the Bonds statute or other law [S:far-28-102-1]. Pursuant to 40 U.S.C. 3132, for construction contracts greater than $35,000 but not greater than $150,000, the contracting officer shall select two or more payment protections from a list of five: a payment bond, an irrevocable letter of credit, a tripartite escrow agreement, certificates of deposit, and a deposit of the types of security listed in FAR 28.204-1 and 28.204-2, giving particular consideration to including the letter of credit [S:far-28-102-1]. The contractor must furnish all bonds or alternative payment protection before receiving a notice to proceed or being allowed to start work [S:far-28-102-1]. The two numbers are not a drafting slip: the acquisition-threshold inflation adjustment in 41 U.S.C. 1908 does not apply to dollar thresholds in sections 3131 through 3134 of title 40, except that any modification of such a threshold made by regulation and in effect on the date that exception was enacted remains in effect [S:usc-41-1908-acquisition-thresholds]. Which figure governs a given solicitation is a question for the contracting officer and for the contract's own clauses.

Federal bonds also constrain who the surety may be. Treasury publishes a list of certificate holding companies annually as of August 1 in Department Circular No. 570, Companies Holding Certificates of Authority as Acceptable Sureties on Federal Bonds and as Acceptable Reinsuring Companies, with information as to underwriting limitations, the areas in which listed sureties are licensed to transact surety business, and other details [S:cfr-31-223-16-treasury-circular-570]. Bonds underwritten by certified companies on that list may be presented to an agency bond-approving official for acceptance; selection among qualified companies is discretionary with the principal required to furnish the bond, and acceptance of a bond by the bond-approving official is subject to 31 CFR 223.17 [S:cfr-31-223-16-treasury-circular-570].

California's contractor license bond is a different animal from a contract bond. Business and Professions Code section 7071.6(a) requires the board, as a condition precedent to the issuance, reinstatement, reactivation, renewal, or continued maintenance of a license, to require that the applicant or licensee file or have on file a contractor's bond in the sum of $25,000 [S:ca-bpc-7071-6-contractor-bond]. CSLB's Fast Facts guide, Rev. 12/22, says the bond or cashier's check is filed for the benefit of consumers who may be damaged because of defective construction or other violations of contractors' state license law and for employees who have not been paid wages they are owed, and that with a contractor license bond a surety company promises the State of California that it will pay damages if the contractor violates contractors' state license law [S:cslb-license-bonds-fast-facts]. Two features surprise people. The bond amount is not per job; the guide says it is the amount available for all the jobs a contractor takes on during the life of the bond, and that once the bond has been depleted a contractor must purchase a new one for the license to remain in effect [S:cslb-license-bonds-fast-facts]. And section 7071.6(b) provides that, excluding claims brought by the beneficiaries specified in subdivision (a) of section 7071.5, the aggregate liability of a surety on claims brought against the bond shall not exceed $7,500; the same subdivision goes on to provide that the bond proceeds in excess of $7,500 shall be reserved exclusively for the claims of those section 7071.5(a) beneficiaries [S:ca-bpc-7071-6-contractor-bond]. The cap and the reservation are one rule, and reading the cap alone makes the remaining $17,500 look unavailable to anyone when the statute has already assigned it. There is also a branch that doubles the number. Section 7071.6(d) provides that, notwithstanding any other law, the board may require an applicant as a condition precedent to licensure to post a contractor's bond in twice the amount required by subdivision (a) until the license is renewed, where the applicant has been convicted of a violation of section 7028 or cited under section 7028.7, where any such citation has been reduced to a final order of the registrar, and where the violation or the basis for the citation constituted a substantial injury to the public [S:ca-bpc-7071-6-contractor-bond]. The guide adds that some license qualifiers, including responsible managing employees, are required to have a $25,000 bond on file, and that CSLB may require a separate disciplinary bond for contractors who have been disciplined [S:cslb-license-bonds-fast-facts].

Three common families, one structure. This is not a complete taxonomy. License and permit bonds, of which the CSLB contractor's bond is one, are required by statute as a condition of holding the license [S:ca-bpc-7071-6-contractor-bond][S:cslb-license-bonds-fast-facts]. Contract bonds are tied to a specific job; NASBP lists the main types of contract surety bonds as bid bonds, performance bonds, payment bonds, and warranty bonds, sometimes called maintenance bonds [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding], and SBA guarantees bid, payment, performance, and ancillary bonds issued by certain surety companies [S:sba-surety-bond-guarantee-program]. Court and judicial instruments sit inside California's classification as well, since the statutory definition of surety insurance expressly reaches bonds and undertakings required or permitted in all actions or proceedings or by law allowed [S:ca-ins-code-105-surety-insurance]. The three-party structure and the principal's reimbursement duty run across all of them.

Bond cost is not priced like a loss-funded insurance rate. NASBP says the cost of a bond is based on rates filed by insurance companies with the state insurance department and on the contract amount, that it can vary from less than 0.5 percent to as much as 3 percent of the contract price, and that a small and emerging contractor with minimal experience can expect to pay 2 to 3 percent of the contract price; it also says bonds must be paid when they are executed and are non-cancelable [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding]. For small businesses, SBA guarantees surety bonds issued by certain surety companies, requires small businesses to pay SBA a fee of 0.6 percent of the contract price on all performance and payment bond guarantees, charges no fee for bid bond guarantees, and covers contracts up to $9 million for non-federal contracts and up to $14 million for federal contracts [S:sba-surety-bond-guarantee-program]. Whether a particular business qualifies for that program, or for a bond at all, is decided by SBA and by the surety, not by a general guide.
whatChanges: Whether the instrument is a contract bond tied to one job or a license bond tied to a licensee's conduct over time. The claimant classes and the amounts differ: SBA's definitions describe bid, performance, payment, and ancillary bonds by their conditions [S:cfr-13-115-10-sba-definitions], while California's contractor's bond is a $25,000 statutory condition of licensure [S:ca-bpc-7071-6-contractor-bond].

The contract value, the awarding body, and where the work is performed. Federal construction above the applicable threshold calls for Miller Act performance and payment bonds, while construction contracts greater than $35,000 but not greater than $150,000 use two or more payment protections selected by the contracting officer; and a contracting officer may waive the bond requirement for work under a contract to be performed in a foreign country on a finding that furnishing the bonds is impracticable for the contractor [S:usc-40-3131-miller-act][S:far-28-102-1].

Whether the contracting officer asks for more than the statute requires. 40 U.S.C. 3131(e) provides that the section does not limit a contracting officer's authority to require a performance bond or other security in addition to the bonds specified in subsection (b), or in cases other than the cases specified there, so the threshold sets when bonds are mandatory rather than what may be demanded [S:usc-40-3131-miller-act].

The bond form itself, because each bond states its own conditions and its own penal sum, and the SBA definitions describe bonds by the event each is conditioned upon rather than by a single universal wording [S:cfr-13-115-10-sba-definitions][S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding].

Whether the surety holds a Treasury certificate of authority. Bonds underwritten by certified companies on the Department Circular No. 570 list may be presented to an agency bond-approving official, and the Circular carries underwriting limitations and the areas in which each listed surety is licensed [S:cfr-31-223-16-treasury-circular-570].

Whether a general agreement of indemnity has been signed and by whom. NASBP says sureties almost always require the principal, the individuals who own or control the company, their spouses, and often affiliated companies to sign it, and that it applies to all bonds the surety issues for that principal [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding].

For a California contractor, whether the license is active, since no bond is required of a holder of a license inactivated on the board's official records during the period it is inactive, and how much of the $25,000 remains, since CSLB says the amount is not per job and a depleted bond must be replaced for the license to remain in effect [S:ca-bpc-7071-6-contractor-bond][S:cslb-license-bonds-fast-facts].
variability: License bond amounts and claimant classes are set state by state by statute. California sets the contractor's bond at $25,000; excluding claims by the beneficiaries specified in section 7071.5(a), it caps a surety's aggregate liability on claims against that bond at $7,500 and reserves the proceeds above $7,500 exclusively for those section 7071.5(a) beneficiaries. The California amount is not fixed for every applicant either: section 7071.6(d) lets the board require twice the subdivision (a) amount, until the license is renewed, from an applicant convicted under section 7028 or cited under section 7028.7 with the citation reduced to a final order, where the violation constituted a substantial injury to the public [S:ca-bpc-7071-6-contractor-bond].

The federal bonding figure reads differently in the statute and in the regulation: 40 U.S.C. 3131(b) says more than $100,000, while FAR 28.102-1(a) states the requirement for any construction contract exceeding $150,000 [S:usc-40-3131-miller-act][S:far-28-102-1]. The general acquisition-threshold inflation adjustment in 41 U.S.C. 1908 does not reach thresholds in 40 U.S.C. 3131 through 3134, except that a modification made by regulation and in effect on the date that exception was enacted remains in effect [S:usc-41-1908-acquisition-thresholds].

Bond pricing is reported by NASBP as based on rates filed by insurance companies with the state insurance department and on the contract amount, ranging from less than 0.5 percent to as much as 3 percent of the contract price, with 2 to 3 percent typical for a small and emerging contractor with minimal experience [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding]. That is one trade association's description of market practice, not a filed rate you can rely on for a specific account.

Which surety a given obligee will accept varies. For federal bonds the acceptance route runs through the Department Circular No. 570 list and is subject to 31 CFR 223.17 [S:cfr-31-223-16-treasury-circular-570]; a California license bond must be on file with CSLB in the statutory amount [S:ca-bpc-7071-6-contractor-bond][S:cslb-license-bonds-fast-facts].

The forum for an unresolved bond dispute depends on the amount and the claimant. CSLB's Rev. 12/22 guide says a consumer who is not satisfied with the surety's response may take the contractor to small claims court for amounts up to $10,000, with claims above that filed in superior court [S:cslb-license-bonds-fast-facts]; that figure is out of date, because Code of Civil Procedure section 116.221 gives the small claims court jurisdiction in an action brought by a natural person if the demand does not exceed $12,500 [S:ccp-116-221-small-claims-limit].
nextActions: Read the document that imposes the bond requirement, whether that is the contract clause, the statute, or the license law section, and then read the bond form itself, including its conditions and its penal sum, rather than a summary of it.

For federal construction work, check whether the proposed surety appears on Treasury's Department Circular No. 570 list and what underwriting limitation and licensed areas the Circular shows for it [S:cfr-31-223-16-treasury-circular-570].

For a California contractor, confirm with CSLB what bond is currently on file and whether a qualifier bond or a disciplinary bond also applies [S:ca-bpc-7071-6-contractor-bond][S:cslb-license-bonds-fast-facts].

Have a lawyer review any general agreement of indemnity before signing it. NASBP says these agreements are almost always signed by the owners, their spouses, and often affiliated companies, and who is bound and to what is a legal question [S:nasbp-32-questions-contract-bonding][S:ca-civ-code-2847-surety-reimbursement].

If bonds are hard to obtain, review the SBA Surety Bond Guarantee Program's fee and contract limits with a surety bond producer, and let SBA and the participating surety decide eligibility [S:sba-surety-bond-guarantee-program].
author: Aaron Bollinger

handoff.reason: The general mechanics can be answered from public statutes, regulations, and regulator guidance, but bonding capacity, which bond form a particular obligee will accept, and the personal exposure created by a general agreement of indemnity are underwriting and legal questions specific to the applicant. A licensed surety bond producer can work through prequalification and how a bond sits alongside the business's other coverage; the indemnity agreement should go to a lawyer before it is signed.
